title: David Walliams goes off-Brand, Libraries Commons is launched, Shropshire cuts, and an AI corruption case in India
author: Ian Anstice / The Library Campaign

editorial.text: Leaving aside the horribleness of the David Walliams case for those involved, it’s been interesting to see how public libraries have dealt with it. Their response has largely been to wait for a national statement from Libraries Connected before doing anything. Purely from publicly available sources (and I know of many more privately), I count 34 services who have kept the disgraced author’s books on their shelves, and just 2 who have taken them off. Somewhat worryingly, it’s been the Far Right who have been the ones most vocal in agreeing with this strategy, with Unherd and Restore being in favour (perhaps showing the truth of the old adage that a stopped clock is correct twice a day) but, apart from this, it’s been great to see library services doing something en bloc together rather than going their own way. I have difficulty thinking this would have been the case twenty years ago and is a tribute to the respect that Libraries Connected has garnered since it was set up that it happened this week. Perhaps herding cats is not impossible, at least some of the time. What would have been the big news this week – Shropshire library cuts and the launch of Library Commons – has to take second place. Shropshire has announced what looks like a quite severe cost-cutting move – it could close two libraries and its mobile, plus cut the hours of six main libraries. One suspects that there will be the usual campaign groups, consultation (possibly even genuine), the attempted volunteerisation of opposition etc in future months so watch out for that. In more positive news, there’s been the launch of a website dedicated to public library data. Well done, as ever, to Libraries Hacked for trying to get something sorted. This is especially important after the largely unexpected loss of LibraryOn but, frankly, has been needed for decades. Considering its stock in trade, it’s always been embarrassing that the public libraries sector has been so rubbish in publishing information about itself and I hope this can change. My thanks to Dave Rowe, the force behind Libraries Hacked, for answering some questions about it below. Finally, public libraries have made big news in India in the last week or two as a massive corruption case has come to light with due to a new library having lots of fake books in it. Fake, that is, because they appear to be AI-written knock-offs. Over seventy thousand books have had to be withdrawn, with five library staff suspended, and the crisis becoming a major political football. This is the first time I’ve seen something like this. Mind you, it’s also been the first time that I’ve seen a library mural with a three-winged parrot included. Yet another AI problem to consider I guess. Whoopee doo.
